title: Decomposing Short-Term Return Reversal
snippet:
The profit to a standard short-term return reversal strategy can be decomposed analytically into four components: 1) across-industry return momentum, 2) within industry variation in expected returns, 3) under-reaction to within-industry cash flow news, and 4) a residual. Only the residual component, which isolates reaction to recent “nonfundamental” price changes, is significant and positive in the data. A simple short-term return reversal trading strategy designed to capture the residual component generates a highly significant risk-adjusted return three times the size of the standard reversal strategy during our 1982-2009 sampling period. Our decomposition suggests that short-term return reversal is pervasive, much greater than previously documented, and driven by investor sentiment on the short side and liquidity shocks on the long side.

Moskowitz and Grinblatt (1999) document a strong industry momentum, in that current winner industries outperform current loser industries in the subsequent month, which implies that the across-industry reversal component will be negative on average. This suggests that the within industry reversal component must be the source of the profits of the standard reversal strategy.

title: Skewness — Why "Same Sharpe" Can Mean "Wildly Different Strategy"
snippet:
Negatively skewed (skewness < 0): A long left tail. Most outcomes are small. Occasional outcomes are large negative surprises. Insurance-like.
...
Hedge funds that sell volatility (think 2018's "VIXmageddon" or any short-vol blowup) look exactly like insurance companies in their good years. Their Sharpe Ratios are spectacular, their max drawdowns are small, their reports are full of awards. Then one event happens and the one monthly return wipes out years of premium collection.

If you only saw their pre-2018 Sharpe Ratio, you'd have allocated. If you'd looked at their skewness, you'd have known something was wrong. Negative skew strategies don't blow up most of the time — they blow up eventually, and the moment you happen to be holding them when they do is fully in the hands of luck.
